# ClearPix — AI Image Restoration

**Deep Learning | CNN Autoencoder | TensorFlow/Keras | Python**

ClearPix restores noisy images with a convolutional neural network (CNN) autoencoder and presents the results in an interactive Streamlit web application. The model learns to reconstruct a clean image from a corrupted one, and is compared against traditional filters (Gaussian blur and non-local means) using PSNR and SSIM.

**Project status:** Implementation complete. Training and evaluation results are generated by `train.py` and `evaluate.py` and written to `results/`.

## Objectives

- Develop a CNN-based autoencoder for image denoising.
- Train and evaluate the model on an appropriate image dataset.
- Compare noisy inputs with restored outputs.
- Evaluate restoration quality with quantitative metrics.
- Build an interactive web interface for testing the trained model.

## Methodology

1. **Dataset preparation:** CIFAR-10 (downloaded automatically) or any folder of your own images, cut into random square patches.
2. **Noise generation:** Gaussian noise with a random standard deviation (default 0.05–0.25) is added to each clean image every epoch, producing fresh noisy–clean pairs.
3. **Model development:** A fully convolutional encoder–decoder in TensorFlow/Keras, with optional skip connections.
4. **Training:** Mean squared error loss, Adam optimizer, learning-rate scheduling, early stopping and best-model checkpointing.
5. **Evaluation:** PSNR and SSIM against the noisy input and two classical baselines, across several noise levels.
6. **Web application:** Upload an image, simulate or supply noise, and compare the input with the restored output.

## Model Architecture

| Stage | Layers | Filters |
|---|---|---|
| Encoder 1 | 2 × (Conv 3×3, BatchNorm, ReLU), MaxPool | 32 |
| Encoder 2 | 2 × (Conv 3×3, BatchNorm, ReLU), MaxPool | 64 |
| Bottleneck | 2 × (Conv 3×3, BatchNorm, ReLU) | 128 |
| Decoder 2 | Upsample, Conv, skip concat, 2 × (Conv, BatchNorm, ReLU) | 64 |
| Decoder 1 | Upsample, Conv, skip concat, 2 × (Conv, BatchNorm, ReLU) | 32 |
| Output | Conv 3×3, sigmoid | 3 |

The network is fully convolutional, so it accepts images of any size. Use `--no-skip` in `train.py` to train a plain autoencoder without skip connections and compare the two.

## Evaluation Metrics

| Metric | Purpose |
|---|---|
| PSNR | Pixel-level reconstruction quality, in dB (higher is better) |
| SSIM | Structural similarity between images, from 0 to 1 (higher is better) |
| Reconstruction loss | MSE between prediction and clean target during training |

`evaluate.py` writes `metrics.csv`, `metrics.json`, `metrics_comparison.png` and `sample_results.png` to `results/`.

## Web Application

- Upload an image and preview it.
- Choose whether the image is clean (noise is added for you) or already noisy.
- Select the noise type (Gaussian, salt & pepper, speckle) and level.
- View original, noisy, restored and classical-filter results side by side.
- See PSNR and SSIM when a clean reference is available.
- Download the restored image.

## Installation and Usage

```bash
git clone https://github.com/Dwaipayan-15/ClearPix-AI-Image-Restoration.git
cd ClearPix-AI-Image-Restoration

python -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate        # Windows: .venv\Scripts\activate
pip install -r requirements.txt
```

**1. Train** (CIFAR-10 by default, about 30 epochs):

```bash
python train.py
# or with your own images
python train.py --data-dir ./my_images --patch-size 64 --epochs 50
```

**2. Evaluate:**

```bash
python evaluate.py
```

**3. Launch the app:**

```bash
streamlit run app.py
```

Training on a GPU (for example in Google Colab) is much faster. Upload the project, run `!pip install -r requirements.txt` and `!python train.py`, then download `models/clearpix_autoencoder.keras` into your local `models/` folder.

## Limitations and Future Scope

- The model is trained on Gaussian noise, so salt-and-pepper and speckle noise are restored less well.
- Training on CIFAR-10 (32×32) limits generalization to high-resolution photographs. Training on patches from your own images improves this.
- Possible improvements: mixed-noise training, perceptual or SSIM-based loss, residual (noise-predicting) learning, and deeper U-Net or DnCNN-style models.
- Deploying the application online (for example on Streamlit Community Cloud).
